narrative:
The model estimated a 98% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In this admissions process, that prediction was strong enough to deny your law school application. This is a forecast, not a certainty, but it means the school judged your current record to indicate very high risk.

The largest influence was your third-year class standing. You are in the lowest decile, while accepted students average around the sixth decile; this pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. The second-largest influence was your LSAT score of 25, compared with an accepted-student average of about 37, which also pushed toward failure. Third was your first-year class standing: again the lowest decile versus an average near the sixth decile, adding further weight toward failure. These academic indicators, not your gender or race, drove the decision.

To improve a future application, focus first on a structured LSAT retake plan and aim for a substantially higher score. Then strengthen your academic record through additional rigorous coursework or a graduate/post-baccalaureate program that shows sustained improvement. Ask admissions whether new evidence can be considered or whether you can receive feedback. Apply to schools that review applications holistically and explain any circumstances behind your early grades.
